text: Good evening, council members. My name is Janet, and I've lived in the Riverside neighborhood for fourteen years. I'm speaking tonight in strong support of the missing-middle zoning reform. Our adult children cannot afford to buy anywhere near the family home, and the teachers, nurses, and mechanics who work in this city keep telling me the same story at my shop. Allowing duplexes and fourplexes along the transit corridors is a modest, sensible change that matches the walkable future we keep saying we want. I know some neighbors worry about parking and congestion, and I share those concerns, but the proposed design standards already address them with tree protections and unit limits. I urge you to approve the ordinance on first reading. Thank you.

I'm David, a renter in the Eastside apartments, and I wholeheartedly support converting the vacant lot on Maple Street into a community garden. For three years that lot has sat fenced and empty while our neighborhood has nowhere to grow food or even meet each other outdoors. The garden proposal includes raised beds, a water tap, and a volunteer stewardship agreement, so the city takes on almost no maintenance cost. My daughter's elementary class has already signed up to run a pollinator bed. This is exactly the kind of low-cost, high-trust project that makes dense neighborhoods livable. Please vote yes on the garden lease and fund the water connection in this year's budget.

Hello, I'm Priya, a homeowner directly adjacent to the proposed Linden Logistics warehouse. I oppose this development as currently designed, and I want the record to show why. The traffic study counts 340 additional truck trips a day, but it never models the intersection my kids cross on their bikes to get to school. Last month an eighteen-wheeler making a delivery to the existing park mounted the curb across from our mailbox. A facility this size will also run diesel reefer units through the night, and our homes already fail the nighttime noise standard on weekends. We are not against jobs; we are against a project whose impacts have been measured everywhere except the street where we live. Please deny the variance.

My name is Marcus and I own a condominium in the Harbor district. I'm asking the council to oppose the ordinance that would legalize whole-home short-term rentals citywide. On my floor alone, three units have been turned into permanent vacation listings, and the building now has rotating strangers in the hallway, broken intercoms, and insurance problems that fall on the rest of us. Long-term rents have climbed eighteen percent in two years, and every unit removed from the rental market makes that worse. The enforcement proposal relies on neighbors filing complaints, which puts the burden on elderly residents who are afraid of retaliation. A pilot zone with strict caps would be defensible; this blanket legalization is not. I urge a no vote.

Good evening. I'm Theresa, a resident of Ward 3, and I'm not here to take a position for or against the water rate adjustment. I have three questions I would like staff to answer before the vote. First, the rate worksheet shows a fixed charge and a volume charge, but I cannot tell from the packet how a typical household's bill changes in dollars. Second, the capital plan mentions lead service line replacement, yet no timeline by street is published. Third, the low-income assistance program is described as existing, but the application numbers in the appendix appear to be missing. I would feel comfortable supporting or opposing this once those questions are answered with documents, not just verbal assurances. Thank you for your time.

I'm Owen, and I run a small accounting practice on Main Street. I come tonight neither supporting nor opposing the municipal broadband proposal; instead I want to share what my clients experience. Roughly a third of the small businesses I serve still have only one wired provider, and their service tickets routinely take more than a week to resolve. At the same time, the business case in the feasibility study assumes a forty percent take rate, which is higher than any comparable municipal network I could find documentation for. My ask is neutral: please publish the sensitivity analysis behind that take rate and the fallback budget if subscriptions fall short. With those numbers in the open, the business community can form a real position.

Hi, I'm Lucia, a cyclist and a grandmother on Birchwood Lane. My feelings about the protected bike lane project are genuinely mixed, and I want to be honest about both sides. I love that my granddaughter would have a safe route to the middle school, and the crash data on this corridor is frightening — three serious injuries last year alone. But the design removes twenty-two on-street parking spaces, and the elderly residents of the Birchwood apartments have nowhere else to park when their caregivers visit. The traffic diversion also pushes cars onto side streets that were never engineered for through traffic. I support building protected lanes in this city, but I cannot support this exact alignment without a parking mitigation plan. Please redesign, don't abandon.

My name is Frank and I've pastored a church two blocks from the proposed navigation center for twenty years. I have a mixed position. Morally, this city needs more shelter capacity, and our church basement has hosted the cold-weather overflow program every winter, so I know the need is real and the residents are our neighbors. However, the proposed site sits between two licensed daycares, and the operational plan before us has no dedicated mental-health staffing after ten at night. The peer cities the consultant cites all staff that model differently. I would enthusiastically support a revised proposal with 24-hour clinical staff and a written walking-route agreement with the daycares. As written, I cannot tell my congregants to endorse it.

Thank you, Mayor. As director of the Housing and Community Development Department, I am recommending that council place the affordable housing bond on the March ballot. Our consolidated housing needs assessment documents a shortage of roughly nine thousand units affordable to households earning below sixty percent of area median income, and private construction at current zoning cannot close that gap within a decade. The bond would fund land assembly, gap financing for nonprofit developers, and a first-time buyer assistance program, all under prevailing-wage requirements. Our office has published the full underwriting, including debt service coverage and the impact on the median tax bill, which comes to approximately thirty-six dollars a year. I'm confident this is a sound and measurable investment, and I'm happy to take questions.

Good evening. I'm the city's sustainability manager, and our office fully supports the proposed electric vehicle charging buildout in public parking facilities. The infrastructure plan uses existing electrical service where possible, which keeps the first-phase cost under four hundred thousand dollars, and the selected vendor assumes all maintenance risk under a ten-year contract. Charging revenue is projected to cover operating costs by year three, and the buildout moves us toward the fleet electrification targets the council adopted two years ago. Equally important, thirty percent of the ports will be installed in the garages serving our lowest-income neighborhoods, so this is not simply an amenity for early adopters. We recommend approval and can begin procurement within thirty days.

Madam Chair, I'm the budget director, and I must formally oppose the amendment that would cut the transit operating subsidy by fifteen percent to fund additional road resurfacing. Our ridership model shows that a cut of that size forces either a twenty-five percent service frequency reduction or a fare increase above the elasticity threshold where net revenue actually declines. The routes most affected are the two crosstown lines that carry essential workers to the hospital and the community college, populations with the lowest car ownership in the city. Road resurfacing has legitimate needs, but they are addressed in the separate pavement bond already before the voters. I recommend rejecting the amendment and keeping the transit subsidy intact.

Chief's office report — good evening. I'm the police department's privacy and technology analyst, and the department opposes the camera expansion ordinance in its current form, which may surprise this chamber. The proposal permits warrantless retention of footage for ninety days across two hundred new locations, including outside a health clinic and a legal aid office. Our own audit of the pilot system found that cameras had no measurable effect on property crime but generated more than four thousand false alerts a month, each consuming analyst time. Expansion without a written retention policy, a public camera map, and independent audit requirements creates legal exposure the city should not accept. We ask that the item be held, not passed.

Thank you for having me. I'm the senior traffic engineer assigned to the Elm Street corridor study, and my role tonight is strictly informational; I am not recommending approval or denial of any project. The study collected twelve weeks of turning-movement counts, transit dwell times, and pedestrian crossings at four intersections. Peak-hour volume currently sits at level of service C at Elm and Third, projected to degrade to level E by 2032 under existing zoning alone. Crash frequency is roughly double the state average for corridors of this width, with sixty percent of incidents involving left turns. The full datasets, including raw counts and confidence intervals, are posted in the meeting packet. I'll present the technical findings and reserve all policy judgments for the commission.

Good evening. As the city's finance director, I'll present the first-quarter revenue report without a recommendation, since policy choices belong to the council. Sales tax receipts came in 3.2 percent above forecast, driven mainly by durable goods, while hotel occupancy tax ran 1.8 percent below, tracking national business-travel trends. Property tax assessments are stable, and the rainy-day balance remains at the policy floor of eight percent of expenditures. What I will flag factually: three of the largest employers have issued lease decisions pending for the third quarter, and each could move either revenue line materially. The tables in your packet show best, base, and downside cases. I'm here to answer technical questions; I take no position tonight.

Thank you. As planning director, I have a mixed recommendation on the industrial-to-residential rezoning, which I want to lay out precisely. The site is well located near the commuter rail station, and converting underused industrial land to housing aligns directly with the comprehensive plan this council adopted last year — on the merits, I support the land-use direction. My reservations are procedural. The environmental site assessment is a Phase One only, with no groundwater testing despite the parcel's prior plating-shop use, and the traffic impact memo relies on 2019 volumes that predate the adjacent warehouse opening. Approve the concept tonight if you wish, but condition any final entitlement on a Phase Two assessment and refreshed traffic counts. I cannot recommend unconditional approval.

Evening. I'm the parks and recreation superintendent, and my position on the Riverside dog park proposal is mixed. From a recreation-equity standpoint, I support it: the west side currently has no off-leash facility, and our resident survey ranked dog parks as the fourth most requested amenity. The proposed five-acre footprint is also land the department already maintains, so no acquisition cost is involved. My concerns are operational. The site drains poorly after rain, and fencing it without a stormwater redesign would create chronic mud and water-quality runoff into the creek. Our staffing model also shows no budget for the daily inspections a dog park requires. Approve the concept, but pair it with the drainage redesign and a maintenance endowment, or the department would have to oppose it later.

Mayor, if I may, the clerk will now read a written statement submitted to the record, the author having requested that their name be withheld. Quote: I am writing to express support for the historic preservation ordinance before the council. As someone who has restored two properties in the old town district, I can say the design-review process is not the burden its critics claim; in my experience it adds weeks, not months, and protects the character that makes our downtown worth visiting. The ordinance's hardship waiver already accommodates owners facing genuinely infeasible costs. Demolition of the remaining nineteenth-century storefronts would be irreversible, while a no vote tonight removes nothing but a layer of review. I ask the council to adopt the ordinance. End quote, and the letter will be filed in the correspondence packet.

Caller, you're live with the council; please state your name for the record. ... Hi, yes, can you hear me? I'd rather not give my last name, I'm just a resident who works evenings. I'm calling in support of the public mural program. The blank walls along the underpass have been covered in tags for years, and every mural the city has commissioned so far actually reduced graffiti cleanup calls on that block — I looked at the neighborhood association minutes. The program uses local artists and a community review panel, so nobody is imposing outside imagery on us. Fifteen thousand dollars for three murals is trivial next to what the city spends painting over vandalism. I hope you fund it. That's all I have, thank you.

The next item is a comment card submitted online under the name 'A Ward 4 commuter,' no contact information verified. Reading as submitted: I oppose the roundabout planned at Fifth and Grove. The simulation videos the engineering firm presented assume drivers will yield correctly, which anyone who commutes this corridor knows is fantasy; the same firm's last roundabout in the county produced twice the predicted fender benders in its first winter. Emergency response times were not modeled for snow conditions at all, and the fire station is three blocks away. The projected delay savings are under twenty seconds per vehicle at enormous construction cost. Please keep the traffic signal and spend that money on sidewalk repairs instead. Submitted for the record.

Speaker at podium three, please proceed, and for the minutes, state your name and affiliation. ... I'm representing a group, I'd prefer not to say which. We oppose the special-use permit for the cannabis dispensary on Oakwood Avenue. The applicant's security plan shows cameras but no armed guard after midnight, and the comparable-operating data comes from a suburb with half our density. The location is within five hundred feet of a youth center, measured along the walking route children actually use, regardless of what the straight-line map says. State law may make outright bans impossible, but a permit is a privilege conditioned on mitigating neighborhood harm, and this application has not met that bar. Deny it pending a revised security and siting analysis. That's our statement.

Next is an anonymous written comment, which staff has confirmed contains factual observations rather than a policy demand. Quote: For the record on the coyote management discussion, I live adjacent to the Greenway and have documented sightingings in a log for eighteen months. Between January and June this year I recorded forty-one sightings, of which four involved animals approaching leashed dogs and none involved unprovoked approach to a person. Den sites were located in two drainage culverts shown on the public works map. I am not asking for culling or against it; I am asking that whatever the council decides be based on logged observations rather than anecdotes, and I will hand the full spreadsheet, with dates and times, to the city wildlife coordinator. No signature. End quote, received through the website portal.

Public comment line six, you have three minutes. ... Hello? Yes, I'm here. I don't want to give my name, and I'm not taking a side on the library budget; I just want to put numbers on the record. I pulled the usage reports the library publishes monthly. Door counts are up nine percent year over year, but program attendance is down four percent, and the only line item that fell in actual spending was materials, while overtime went up. Sunday hours account for the entire new overtime request, yet Sunday door counts average forty percent below weekdays. I'm not saying cut anything; I'm saying the discussion about restoring hours should use these specific figures rather than general claims about usage. The reports are public and anyone can reproduce what I did. Thank you.

Written comment, author lists only 'a small-business owner on Lexington Avenue,' no further identification. Reading: My view on the food-truck ordinance is mixed and I won't pretend otherwise. As a customer, I support more street food; the trucks bring evening foot traffic that the avenue lost when the big anchor closed, and several truck owners are local graduates of the city's kitchen incubator. As a leaseholder paying property taxes and a fixed rent, however, I cannot ignore that trucks occupy the metered spaces my customers use while bearing none of my buildout or utility costs, and the current draft has no cap on how many can cluster per block. I would support the ordinance with a per-block cap, a permit fee that reflects infrastructure use, and designated staging rather than ad hoc parking. Without those terms, I oppose it. Filed.

Anonymous voicemail left on the public comment line, transcribed by staff. I have mixed feelings about the stormwater fee and wanted them on record. On one hand, the flooding in my basement has gotten worse three years running, and the engineers' map shows my block is in the highest-priority basin, so I get why new revenue is needed and I'm not anti-tax. On the other hand, the fee is structured per impervious surface, which means renters in apartment buildings pay nothing directly while elderly homeowners on fixed incomes get the whole bill, and nothing in the ordinance requires the housing authority to pass through any incentive. Fix the equity structure, give low-income seniors a deferral, and I'll support it. As drafted, I'd vote no if I could vote at all. End of message.

Uh, evenin council, my name is Dolores, I live on Kester Ave, got the letter about the rezoning and I gotta oppoze it plain and simple. We been here thirty-two years and every time the city says infill, what we recievd was more traffic and less parking and nobody from planning ever knocks on our doors after. The devlopment packet says the school capacity is fine, but my grandkids class already has twenty-nine kids in a trailer, so somebody's numbers dont add up. They say trees will be replaced but the last project replaced forty-year oaks with saplings tied to stakes, half of em dead inside a year. Im not against housing, Im against being treated like the block that always absorbs the costs. Please turn it down till the school study is redone. Thank you.

THIS IS THE DEPUTY CITY MANAGER FOR THE RECORD, ADDRESSING THE AMBULANCE SERVICE CONTRACT. THE DEPARTMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTS AWARDING THE CONTRACT AND I WANT THE RATIONALE ON THE RECORD BEFORE THE VOTE. RESPONSE TIME MEDIANS HAVE MISSED THE CONTRACTUAL TARGET FOR SIX CONSECUTIVE MONTHS UNDER THE INCUMBENT, AND THE PROPOSED VENDOR COMMITS IN WRITING TO NINE MINUTES CITYWIDE WITH LIQUIDATED DAMAGES ATTACHED. THE TRANSITION PLAN KEEPS ALL CURRENT DISPATCH STAFF AND REQUIRES NO CHANGE TO THE 911 CALL ROUTING, SO RESIDENTS SEE NO SERVICE GAP. YES THE BID IS FOUR PERCENT HIGHER, BUT THE PER-CALL PENALTY STRUCTURE MEANS UNDERPERFORMANCE PAYS THE CITY BACK. I RECOMMEND APPROVAL TONIGHT AND CAN SIGN THE TRANSITION ORDER TOMORROW. THANK YOU MAYOR.

Um, hi, yeah, thank you, sorry. So I'm, uh, I'm Brett, I rent over on, on Fulton, and honestly I don't, I don't have a position tonight, like for or against? I just, um, I wanted to ask about the, the thing in the packet, the rental inspection program? Because, you know, my landlord already does kind of whatever, and I'm, I'm confused whether inspections are complaint-based or scheduled, because the handout says both in different places. And, uh, also what happens to a tenant if, if the unit fails and the landlord just evicts instead of fixing? Nobody, like, nobody could tell me at the door. So I'm neutral, I'm not asking you to vote no, I just, I need those two answers in writing before this gets to second reading. That's, that's it, thank you, sorry.

Submitted comment card, name illegible, primarily in Spanish with an English closing note; staff is reading the text as received. 'Buenas noches, solo quiero dejar constancia de los datos de mi cuadra: en los ultimos seis meses se han reportado tres inundaciones en la calle 14, el agua llega hasta las escaleras de las casas, y la alcantarilla frente al numero 212 nunca se ha limpiado durante ese tiempo. No pido que aprueben ni rechacen el proyecto de drenaje hoy; pido que estas fechas y estos numeros se incluyan en el expediente tecnico.' The English note reads: 'I am not saying yes or no to the drainage project. I am asking that my dated flooding observations be entered into the technical file before anyone decides. Thank you.' No signature; card number 44.

Thank you, chair. As the interim water resources manager, my assessment of the reservoir expansion is mixed, and given the truncated time I'll be direct. The supply modeling is sound — our drought curves show a seventy percent chance of mandatory restrictions by 2030 without additional storage, so I support the engineering direction. But the cost-sharing annex attached to tonight's version shifts thirty percent of capital cost to the two smallest districts, and my office was not consulted on that change before— [recording ends mid-sentence; the speaker's remaining remarks and conclusion were not captured. The clerk notes the item was continued to the next session and a written supplement was promised by—

hi I'm Carla I've lived on Gibson since 2009 and I strongly support the sidewalk repair levy because my mother uses a walker and right now she literally cannot get from our porch to the bus stop without someone helping her over three cracked slabs and a utility pole planted in the middle of the path and this isn't a luxury it's the difference between her leaving the house independently or staying inside all week the city's own audit rated forty percent of neighborhood sidewalks as failing and yet repair has been deferred for six straight budgets the levy costs the average household less than a coffee a week and every project is publicly listed with completion dates so we can actually check the work I'm asking every member to vote yes and stop deferring basic access thank you

Good evening. I'm Renata, a parent of two elementary students, and I strongly support restoring evening and Sunday library hours. Last winter our apartment lost heating for a week, and the library was the only warm, quiet place where my children could do homework and I could finish job applications after my shift. Usage data already shows the branches with Sunday hours run at eighty percent capacity, so this is not speculative demand. The cost is modest relative to the overall budget, and the staffing plan draws from existing part-time pools rather than new full-time positions. Restoring these hours is an investment in equitable access for shift workers and crowded households. I urge you to approve the funding. Thank you for your time.

Thank you, Mayor. As the city procurement officer, I oppose the sole-source amendment for the downtown security camera contract. Sole-source awards bypass the competitive bidding requirements written into our municipal code, and the justification memo provides no evidence that only one vendor can meet the technical specifications. The three-year price is twenty-two percent above the average of comparable contracts in peer cities, yet the amendment locks in that rate without a most-favored-customer clause. My office also found the vendor's data-handling terms conflict with the privacy ordinance the council passed just last session. A competitive request for proposals can be issued within forty-five days without any service interruption. I recommend rejecting the amendment and directing staff to bid it properly.

Hello, I'm Sam, a resident and small cafe owner on Court Street. I'm not here to support or oppose the new parking meter policy; I want better information first. The downtown association's survey claims merchants lost twelve percent of sales after meters were installed, but the survey has no control blocks and overlaps with the highway construction that reduced all traffic that summer. Meanwhile the city's sensor data shows turnover doubled, which should help customers find spaces, but nobody has published whether that translated into more short visits to shops. My request is simple: extend the comment period, release the raw sensor data, and compare metered blocks against the two unmatched comparison streets. Once we separate meter effects from construction effects, merchants like me can take a defensible position.

Good evening. I'm the city arborist, and the urban forestry division supports the tree protection ordinance as drafted. Canopy cover has declined from thirty-one to twenty-four percent in fifteen years, and the ordinance finally gives staff a permitting tool before removal rather than a fine after the fact. The proposed replacement ratios are calibrated to species and size, so developers cannot satisfy the rule with tiny saplings, and the hardship waiver protects homeowners facing genuine structural conflicts. Our division has budgeted for the additional inspection load within the existing fee revenue, so the ordinance is cost-neutral to the general fund. The science linking canopy cover to stormwater management and summer temperatures is well established. We recommend passage and stand ready to implement.

Written submission from an unnamed participant via the public portal; identity not verified. Quote: My position on the demolition-delay bylaw is mixed. I support the principle that buildings over a century old deserve a public review before demolition, because the town has already lost most of its mill-era fabric and each teardown is permanent. But the twelve-month delay as written has no mediation requirement and no defined endpoint if the owner and commission simply never agree, which leaves property in legal limbo and invites litigation the town loses more often than not. I would support a six-month delay with mandatory mediation sessions and a hard sunset after which the permit issues automatically. I cannot support the bylaw as currently drafted, though I support its goal. End quote, filed without contact information.
